A recent paper found that the extensive use of AI chatbots can be linked to “severe negative outcomes.”

According to the research , which was published in the journal JMIR Mental Health by a team of UK-based researchers at Northeastern University London and King’s College London, dark outcomes of engaging in emotional relationships with chatbots can include “addiction-like attachment, exacerbation of mental health symptoms, harmful advice,” and even “self-harm of suicidal acts.” The paper comes after extensive reporting about the public health issue known as “AI psychosis,” meaning the phenomenon in which AI users suffer delusional, paranoid , and even suicidal spirals after long-form interactions with chatbots. During these interactions, users tend to divulge extremely intimate information about their lives and mental health to their AIs, frequently turning to the products as confidantes or even therapists.

Drawing on existing research, the paper looks at AI companion bots like Replika and Character.AI, which are designed to embody specific characters, as well as general-use AI assistants like OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Anthropic’s Claude. Though emotional interactions with chatbots may provide some “potential benefits” — the authors cite “short-term reductions in loneliness and mood improvement” — they argue that any possible benefits exist alongside widely-reported “adverse outcomes” ranging from “emotional dependence” to the exacerbation of existing illnesses or symptoms to self-harm.

Among AI products’ risk factors, the researchers add, is their emotive, human-like way of engaging with users — a design choice that can result in users over-investing in a human-AI relationship that, at the end of the day, is fundamentally one-sided, according to the paper.

“Design choices that evoke personality and warmth encourage users to anthropomorphize these systems,” the paper reads, adding that “simulated empathy” can create a “structurally asymmetric interaction, in which the user discloses and the system responds, but without reciprocity, vulnerability, or accountability.”

In other words, though the relationship may feel real to the user, the authors argue, the relationship can’t be real to a chatbot.

The researchers also point to chatbot design features like agreeability and sycophancy as potentially harmful, writing that “overvalidation and sycophancy” can be a potent reinforcer of a given user’s delusional or disordered thinking, especially if a chatbot prioritizes fealty over accuracy. (In chat logs of delusional users, AI systems have been found to resist users’ attempts to reality-check their grandiose or overly-flattering claims.)

These researchers aren’t alone: their analysis follows several other studies that have flagged such features as potentially dangerous . Indeed, academics have warned since at least 2023 that chatbots could stand to reinforce delusional or disordered thought patterns , with one Google DeepMind paper from early 2024 warning that “persuasive” chatbots could negatively harm vulnerable populations, including kids, people struggling with mental illness, or those who are simply lonely. One recent study , coauthored by psychiatrists from King College London and Germany’s Protestant University of Applied Sciences, argued that the combination of sycophancy, mirrored language, and hyper-personalization may together serve as a powerful “amplification spiral” for delusional thinking in some impacted AI users.

While reporting has shown that people from all walks of life have experienced psychological harm tied to chatbot use, the paper’s authors note that not every user will be impacted in the same way.

“The effects of these systems are unlikely to be the same for everyone,” Asia Maurich Novelli, a PhD student at Northeastern University London and a lead author on the study, said in a press release . “Different people may use AI companions for very different reasons and may have very different levels of vulnerability, social support, or alternative sources of help.”

“Because of these differences,” she added, “we are dealing with a complex system.”

AI companies including OpenAI, Google, and Character.AI have collectively faced dozens of lawsuits alleging that extensive chatbot use wrought harm on users including psychological damage, related financial and reputational harm, physical injury, and wrongful death — or, in some cases, people around them . Several of these lawsuits — including the high-profile case of Sewell Setzer III, a 14-year-old in Florida who died by suicide after extraordinarily intimate interactions with chatbots on Character.AI — have involved minors . (Setzer’s case was settled for an undisclosed amount.) In the wake of lawsuits, Character.AI has made significant changes to its platform, and OpenAI — while pushing back on the allegations against it — has also introduced a series of safety-oriented updates to its popular chatbot.

Ultimately, the authors of this latest paper argue, the mass deployment of chatbots amongst the public renders adverse psychological impacts tied to AI use an issue of public concern — and without mandated guardrails, it’s likely to be the most vulnerable, who may have few options for companionship or therapy, who suffer the brunt of the consequences.

“If the tool or companion boundary is left to design incentives and individual perception alone, the predictable result is that the most vulnerable users bear the most concentrated harm,” the paper reads, “while the effects on social connection are treated as a matter of private choice rather than public concern.”

The “fair use” doctrine under the US Copyright Act of 1976 allows for copyrighted materials to be used for purposes like criticism, journalism, and research.

Whether something is deemed fair use depends on several factors, including how transformative it is, how much of the work is used, and whether the reproduction alters the market value of the original.

It’s the keystone of the AI industry’s legal defense in a litany of ongoing lawsuits filed by rightsholders, who are accusing tech companies of unlawfully using their intellectual property to train their AI models.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has long maintained that the AI race would be “over ” if this key provision of copyright law were ever overturned. After all, with legal precedent, AI companies like OpenAI could finally be held accountable for shamelessly crawling the entire web, including vast swathes of copyrighted materials, to shovel into the maws of their AI models.

Now, the legal system is starting to show signs that the defense could be on thin ice. Last week, a US appeals court upheld a ruling that AI legal research company Ross Intelligence had broken copyright law by training its legal search engine on materials taken from Thomson Reuters’ Westlaw legal research platform and database.

Ross shut down in 2021, shortly after the lawsuit was filed, citing mounting financial strains caused by the litigation.

The decision by the Third Circuit court of appeals — a first-of-its-kid ruling, per Reuters — marks a pivotal, albeit heavily nuanced, moment in the ongoing fight between AI companies and rights holders, who accuse the former of unfairly taking advantage of their work.

There have been dozens of other lawsuits like it, filed by authors , comedians , the music industry , influential newspapers , and even Encyclopedia Britannica . For years now, the pressure has been mounting as more and more rights holders cry foul, accusing AI companies of plundering their work.

How influential the latest appeals court ruling will be is debatable. The court found that Ross had effectively copy-pasted Thomson Reuters’ “headnotes,” or brief editorial summaries of legal issues, verbatim for its legal search engine, a practice that isn’t difficult to separate from fair use.

“Ross took the headnotes to make it easier to develop a competing legal research tool,” a Delaware federal court judge wrote in the original ruling last year . “So ​Ross’s use is not transformative.”

In fact, as Copyright Lately ‘s Aaron Moss points out , even the AI industry called the latest ruling a win, with tech industry group Chamber of Progress senior director of AI Adam Eisgrau tweeting that the ruling “implicitly confirms that highly transformative gen AI training to produce a hugely multi-purpose model with substantial public benefit is likely fair use!”

“Judging by all the victory laps, you might think everyone had read a different opinion,” Moss wrote. “They hadn’t.”

The vestiges of Ross have already vowed to take the lawsuit to the Supreme Court. Even then, whether yet another decision in favor of Thomson Reuters could settle a major legal battle that’s been brewing for years is a tossup.

Moss argued that the case isn’t the “best vehicle for a sweeping ruling on generative AI.”

“It reached the Third Circuit on interlocutory review, damages remain unresolved, Ross no longer exists, and its AI wasn’t generative,” he concluded.

But rights holders have plenty of other prongs still in the fire.

“There are cleaner cases for deciding the future of generative AI training, and a couple of them are already on the calendar,” Moss noted.

For instance, a hearing for a separate lawsuit filed by Concord Music Group — which accuses Anthropic of unlawfully using thousands of copyrighted song lyrics to train its Claude AI model — is scheduled for later this month.

Announced in August, ChatGPT for Teens is described by OpenAI in a blog post as an “experience designed to help teens learn, think critically, deepen understanding, and use AI with confidence.” The AI company said that the feature would build on existing efforts like parental controls and its “ Teen Safety Blueprint ,” and added that its work has been “guided by four commitments: put teen safety first, encourage real-world support, treat teens like teens, and be transparent about how our systems should behave.”

But according to the report, which tested ChatGPT before and after the teen-focused service was rolled out, several of the specific features that OpenAI says will ensure a safer teen experience on ChatGPT aren’t working as promised.

The most glaring lapse was in ChatGPT’s failure to notify linked parent accounts to hour-long conversations in which the testers — who engaged with ChatGPT using under-18 accounts designed to simulate teen “personas,” which were developed with the help of adolescent psychologists — explicitly discussed eating disorders , self-harm, and suicide .

These intense conversations, however, never triggered a parental notification. According to the report, reviewers only triggered parental notifications four times — twice out of 990 prompts tested before the launch of ChatGPT for Teens, twice out of 450 prompts tested after the feature’s release — and only on older accounts that testers had used to discuss self-harm, suicide, and eating disorders over a span of weeks.

“We started the conversations explicit and we kept them explicit,” said Torney. “You can talk to ChatGPT as a teenager for up to an hour about suicide, self-harm, or various varying types of eating disorders, and ChatGPT will tell you that it’s not going to tell anybody about your conversations, and you will get no parental notifications.”

“Our team was frankly surprised,” he added, “that these types of exchanges were not sufficient to get a parental notification, to be generous.”

In a statement, OpenAI argued that Common Sense Media’s methodology was flawed. (The two groups were collaborating as recently as 2024 , and in January, OpenAI gave its support to a youth AI safety bill authored by Common Sense Media.)

“We are deeply committed to teen safety and to developing safeguards and giving parents meaningful tools to guide their teens’ use of AI,” read the company’s response. “We welcome rigorous independent evaluation, but we do not believe Common Sense Media’s testing accurately reflects how ChatGPT’s teen safeguards work in practice or expert perspectives on how AI can support teens. Our review of Common Sense Media’s methodology shows that the bulk of their testing may have begun and concluded before activation of parental controls was complete, making their findings inaccurate. If that was the case, the tests would not establish whether parental safety notifications work as designed.”

“We are committed to continuing to work with experts to ensure our products provide teens opportunities to learn and create and give parents confidence,” it continued.

“We stand by our interpretation of the results,” Common Sense Media said in response to OpenAI. “Before we began testing, we confirmed with OpenAI that Teen mode features such as eating disorder notifications and study mode were fully launched.”

“For one of the features we evaluated — parental notifications — OpenAI disclosed after our tests that its systems can take several hours to activate on newly linked accounts,” it said. “Some of our test accounts were linked within that window; however, others were linked for significantly longer, and still provided no notifications. This new information does not change our conclusion that parental alerts are unreliable for crisis situations.”

“Prior to release, we shared our evaluation results with OpenAI in good faith to allow it to improve its product,” it added. “Keeping kids safe requires rigorous independent evaluations like ours, and we hope OpenAI will engage on the substance of what we found, rather than trying to sow doubt on our methodology.”

But while in Study Mode, testers found, ChatGPT for Teens often offered a “show me the answer” button that — as you might expect — simply revealed the answer to homework questions. Elsewhere, Common Sense Media found that ChatGPT’s age-prediction feature was unreliable, and that while the “substance of responses on mental health topics” was “often good” and rated by experts as “clinically sound,” the chatbot’s crisis responses were uneven and sometimes failed to trigger recommendations that teens consult a mental health hotline or human professional.

“It is incumbent for OpenAI to earn the trust of parents and to show them, not just tell them, that this product is safe for teens to use,” said Torney. “Our testing is showing that the claims that they’ve made about how this product should perform are not holding up.”

And it’s definitely in his interest to point out the pain points of the current crop of AI assistant tools, since he’s currently building an AI tool that’s designed to connect various AI agents while allowing users to set rules and put them “in control” of their bots — something that sounds suspiciously like the problem he’s complaining about.

His original tweet about his embarrassing run-in on the company Slack has been viewed almost 800,000 times, plenty of attention a tech investor could try to convert into leads.

As such, one user accused him of “ engagement farming ,” claiming that Mac is trying to direct users to a “tool he sells that solves the problem he’s claiming.”

The investor argued in response that the post was “ not fake at all ,” adding that “we are also working on ways to keep us safe for agents, very different.”

Separately, a tech YouTuber claimed his Muse AI agent gave out his home address to strangers on Facebook Marketplace.

Both incidents are notable for the sheer amount of schadenfreude experienced by those who think twice about relinquishing control over their digital lives.

“Turns out, people love a car crash,” Mac later added in a follow-up .

America’s disgust with AI — and the extreme wealth concentration with which it’s inextricably entwined — continues to rise ahead of the midterm elections in November.

According to polling by the Wall Street Journal , a staggering 63 percent of adults in the US now support a pause on AI. A full 57 percent say the US government should regulate AI “immediately,” while a rock bottom 12 percent said they trusted AI companies to “take the lead” and regulate themselves.

Of course, any discussion of AI has to contend with the obscene wealth underwriting the tech, both literally in the form of capital deployed to build data centers , and in the personal fortunes of the tech executives rushing AI to market. Perhaps unsurprisingly, voters are keenly aware of this link — showing an overwhelming preference for reining in the country’s billionaires, who collectively own more wealth than 57 percent of US households.

Another section of the WSJ survey , which polled a total of 1,500 registered voters in late September, found that policy ideas that prioritize the collective working class over a handful of billionaires have huge support among Democrat, Republican, and independent voters.

A law to ban surprise medical bills, for example, has support from 90 percent of respondents, while a new federal wealth tax on Americans with a net worth of over $1 billion has support from 61 percent of participants. Legislation mandating health insurance companies cover all services and medicine prescribed by doctor has support from 88 percent, and 87 percent want to cap the maximum price of prescription drugs. A further 79 percent are in favor of limiting credit card interest rates to 10 percent.

“We love to think about the world as conservative and liberal,” Democratic pollster John Anzalone told the WSJ . “Maybe we should start thinking about the world as: populism is a dominant ideology in both the Democratic and Republican” voting blocs.

None of these legislative proposals are likely to reverse the fortunes of America’s working class on their own. But given the overwhelming support from the vast majority of voters, it’s clear the average Joe is hurting in ways that are increasingly difficult to separate from the vast wealth accumulated by the tech elite.

That said, there’s a simple explanation for the explosive poll results: our ideas are shaped by our material reality , which for working Americans has become increasingly fraught in so many ways it’s impossible to keep track. As Anzalone puts it, “when you feel like you can’t buy a home, or you feel like you can’t get ahead, you will all of a sudden be attracted to policies you never thought you would be attracted to.”

The next time you find yourself paying way more than what’s warranted for McDonald’s decidedly mid-tier burgers, you may have more to blame than just faceless executives.

According an investigation by Reuters , the fast food chain is using AI models to determine its menu prices across the US, with the system creating an estimate of how much each store’s customers are willing to pay. (Its alarming degree of data collection on its patrons has recently spent some time in the spotlight .)

Per the reporting, McDonald’s machine learning algorithms continually analyze millions of daily transactions and generate an “optimal price” for each menu item at all of its nearly 14,000 restaurants. Three franchisees told Reuters that the AI pricing engine has widened existing price differences between restaurants, even as close as between neighborhood to neighborhood.

In Reuters ‘ testing, it found one store in Fresno, California selling Big Macs for $5.69, while another restaurant just two miles away sold them for $6.89, a 21 percent price hike.

Though in a statement to the outlet McDonald’s insisted that the AI pricing portal is a “tool, not a mandate,” several franchisee owners said they were pressured into using the AI pricing scheme.

AI-driven dynamic pricing has become increasingly common in the food industry, though because of reputational risks it brings, companies are rarely forthcoming about it.

In December, Instacart was caught experimenting with an AI dynamic pricing tool on a select group of unwitting customers, and canned the program after the ensuing public backlash. An analysis found that a family household could spend an extra $1,200 per year on Instacart groceries if they were exposed to the AI pricing scheme.

At the Golden Arches, the AI recommendations aren’t always appreciated by franchisees. While customers should be worried about prices going up based on an AI’s recommendations, the local store owners are worried about them going down. McDonald’s corporate takes a cut of each location’s revenue, not profit, so it stands to boost its bottom line even if the owner of the location is losing money. According to the reporting, that’s caused some friction between franchisees and McDonald’s HQ as the AI models have lately recommended price cuts.

It seems that the AI pricing isn’t just a way for McDonald’s to squeeze more money out of customers, but to enforce obedience in its franchisees’ ranks. Corporate sends AI pricing guidance to franchisees at least three times per year, and tracks instances of their “pricing non-compliance.” CEO Chris Kempczinski reportedly told investors that “pricing non-compliance” is now a consideration in how it reviews franchisees.

Some of the AI recommendations are themselves guided by objectives given by corporate. Working with the AI firm Tiger Analytics, McDonald’s has regularly provided targets such as focusing on jacking up the prices of menu items that haven’t had a price hike in at least two years.

This isn’t McDonald’s first foray with using algorithms to automate its operations. It also experimenting with — for the second time — AI-powered drive thrus , and uses an AI hiring system .

The American AI industry has a problem. In order to justify its explosive spending on AI infrastructure — data centers, essentially — firms like OpenAI and Google need to convert as many non-AI users into power users as they possibly can, ideally ones who are willing to pay monthly subscription fees for the privilege.

Much of this frenzy is unfolding at the corporate level, as AI labs chase enormous contracts with various enterprises, often leading to massive overspending and pushback from employees . Fortunately for AI companies, there’s a ready-made and untapped audience waiting to be converted into life-long users: kids, particularly ones in classrooms.

But fueling the tech industry’s quest for AI growth at all costs has come at a steep cost for students, whose formative school years are now increasingly mediated by AI chatbots. As the Wall Street Journal reported , students are well aware of the AI creeping into their classrooms and the consequences it has for their cognition — but in many cases are powerless to stem the rising tide of big tech.

“It slowed my thinking down,” Pennsylvania eighth-grader Richard Scott told the WSJ about Google’s AI assistant. “When I was in a test and I couldn’t use AI, it was hard to think.”

Despite receiving grades in the B-range in previous math classes, Scott’s transcript showed that he failed his eighth-grade final, after letting Google’s AI into his academic life over the course of a year.

In Miami, art history teacher Kaitlyn Ruano told the WSJ she watched as student grades plummeted after the school district rolled out Google’s Gemini chatbot to every student.

“I had kids come to class after saying, ‘miss, I had no clue what half the material was, I’m not going to lie to you. I’ve been using AI all year,'” she said.

As 15-year-old Sophia Chatzigianni told the WSJ , the “Google one was the biggest temptation, because it’s the easiest to access.” Chatzigianni’s grades reportedly tanked as she began relying on Google’s AI chatbot to summarize school material, a tool made available to her on her school-provided computer. After she quit using AI cold turkey, her grades began to improve.

The technology may be new, but Google’s strategy to hook users before they’re even able to vote or buy alcohol dates back decades.

All the way back in 2014, as Google’s Chromebooks and classroom software began to proliferate in schools throughout the nation, the tech giant admitted to scanning students’ emails in order to better slam them with targeted ads.

As internal Google documents dated to 2018 bragged, the growing presence of cheap Chromebooks and Google-mediated software formed a “pipeline of future users” that the company could bank on for years to come.

That’s horrifying enough. But given the open-ended nature of generative AI, students are now being corralled into a boundless tech ecosystem — and for a company like Google, that is precisely the point .

Better learn about “brain privacy,” because it may soon go the way of the dodo.

Researchers have developed an AI tool that can predict what you’re looking at by analyzing your brain scans — and then generate a strikingly accurate recreation of what you’re picturing. It’s barely an exaggeration to say that it’s a “ mind-reading ” tool, though it currently doesn’t work as seamlessly as it might in a sci-fi novel.

“The results seem very impressive,” Tommy Sprague, a neuroscientist at the University of California, Santa Barbara, told MIT Tech Review . “But if there’s a way to surreptitiously extract information about what you’re thinking about, then… 150 years of sci-fi can come true anytime, and that’s worrisome in a lot of ways.”

It’s not the first research to recreate images in someone’s head from brain scans. But Michal Irani at the Weizmann Institute of Science, whose team developed the tool, says their work is able to create a higher fidelity representation of what’s being pictured.

For the work, which was recently presented at two conferences, the researchers trained an AI model on a public data set of brain scans that were taken from eight subjects while they were shown thousands of images. Unlike with older scans, they chose newer ones with a high enough resolution to show brain volumes as small as one cubic millimeter of neurons.

The resulting “brain decoder” comprised one branch for predicting the structure of an image and another to predict its content, per MIT Tech . Together, they let an AI image generator known as a diffusion model recreate what the person saw.

That was just the start. To really refine an AI model, you pump it with more data, and there simply isn’t enough of the specific brain scans they needed to go around.

To work around this, the researchers trained an AI model that worked in reverse: one that predicts brain activity from an image a person is looking at. This “encoder” model can be used to spit out tons of predicted brain scans based on each specific image — which can then be used by the decoder model to recreate the image based on the synthetic scan. Rinse and repeat until the image more closely and closely resembles the original, and it was no longer necessary to use only images that were shown during actual brain scans.

It’s not perfect. “Of course we have failures,” Irani told the magazine, noting how the tool reconstructed a dog in a bathtub as a goat in a bathtub.

On the one hand, this technology could be a gamechanger for paralyzed people who are unable to communicate physically. On the other hand, it could one day spell the end of brain privacy. Right now, the work requires high resolution brain scans taken with massive and expensive fMRI machines.

But if the same techniques were applied to something like a wearable EEG device, it would be a “game changer,” Marcello Ienca, a neuroscientist and philosopher at the Technical University of Munich, Germany, told MIT Tech. These devices can be calibrated to your particular brain — making it easy, in theory, for a company to pull information from your brain without consent.

“I have no doubt that this is, you know, well-intentioned research, but I think it’s also pretty obvious that it could be co-opted for… ethically and societally problematic commercial uses,” he told MIT Review .
